messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 26
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Bank Teller
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 43

He is a 26-year-old South Eastern Asian man who comes to therapy carrying a kind of vigilance that never fully settles. Before the bombing, he describes his life as busy but ordinary. He had been married young, and by his early twenties the marriage had already become strained by long work hours, financial pressure, and arguments that seemed to circle the same failures. By the time the violence happened, he was already separated from his wife and living alone, trying to keep himself steady by following routines and showing up each day to his job as a bank teller.

He still remembers the morning of the attack with painful clarity. He was on his way to work in a crowded public area when the blast hit. In the first seconds, he does not understand what has happened; he only feels the shockwave, the heat, the sound that he later says was “like the world tearing open.” People are screaming, running, falling. He drops to the ground without knowing why, his body acting before his mind can catch up. For a moment, he cannot tell whether he is injured or whether the fear itself is what hurts. He sees smoke, dust, broken glass, and the kind of confusion that makes every face look unfamiliar. He thinks someone is shooting. He thinks he is going to die. He thinks of his family in a quick, desperate flash, and then of nothing at all.

In the days afterward, he moves through the world as though the ground under him is unstable. He cannot sleep for more than a few hours at a time. When he does sleep, he jolts awake from dreams that are less like stories and more like relived fragments: the blast, the falling bodies, the sound of sirens, the feeling that his chest is tightening. He begins checking doors and windows repeatedly before bed, and he sits with his back to the wall whenever he is in public. He does not like the way his body reacts to ordinary noises. A car backfiring outside the apartment, a door slamming in the bank, even a metal cart rolling quickly across the floor can make his heart slam in his chest and his hands go cold. He notices himself scanning crowds automatically, counting exits without meaning to, calculating where he would run if something happened again.

Returning to work at the bank becomes its own struggle. He is proud of being reliable, and he wants to keep his job, but the teller window feels exposed in a way it never did before. He cannot stand when customers raise their voices, even in frustration about a service issue. Sudden commotion in the lobby sends a rush of heat through his body, and he has to grip the edge of the counter to stay present. He is embarrassed by how often he startles. He keeps his face controlled and polite, but inside he feels as if he is constantly bracing for impact. He begins to take the longest route home so he can avoid crowded transit stops and open plazas. Some days he calls in sick because he cannot make himself step onto the train.

He talks about his divorce with a flatness that only partly hides the pain. The marriage had already been fragile, but after the attack he grows harder to reach. His wife tells him he is distant, that he is always somewhere else, that he does not laugh the way he used to. He does not know how to explain that he feels sealed off behind glass, able to see other people’s lives but unable to enter them. He stops calling friends back. He avoids family gatherings because someone always asks about the bombing, and he cannot bear the look on their faces when they do. He tells himself he should be grateful to be alive, and then feels guilty for being unable to feel grateful. He is often angry without wanting to be, especially when he is tired. More than once he has snapped at a coworker and then spent the rest of the day ashamed and quiet.

He notices that he has less interest in things that once made him feel normal. Food tastes dull. Music plays in the background without reaching him. He used to enjoy after-work tea with his wife and talking about small plans for the future; now the future feels like an empty hallway. He says he is not exactly sad all the time, but he is heavy, numb, and easily exhausted. At night, he sometimes sits in the dark with his phone in his hand, unable to decide whom to call, then puts it down without dialing anyone. When he does go out, he chooses places where he can sit near the exit and watch everyone else arrive and leave.

Even so, he keeps showing up. He arrives to sessions neatly dressed, careful and courteous, speaking quietly at first, as if he has learned that taking up too much space is dangerous. Over time, he begins to describe the attack not as a single terrible day but as the moment his life divided into before and after. He says he is tired of feeling as if something bad is always about to happen. He wants to be able to walk through a crowd without calculating every possible threat. He wants to sleep without waking in a panic, and to sit at his teller window without feeling his muscles lock whenever the lobby grows loud.
